claims.statement: The earliest writing implies trained specialists, but their identities, recruitment and institutional status are poorly recoverable.
claims.counterevidence: Lists and handwriting variation provide indirect evidence, not biographies.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: The best archaeological evidence for formal curricula comes from later household and institutional contexts, especially the Old Babylonian period.
claims.counterevidence: Later evidence cannot be projected unchanged onto Uruk.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: Edubba was not necessarily a single standardized temple-run school system across Mesopotamian history.
claims.counterevidence: Literary school texts use institutional language, but excavated teaching often occurs in houses.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: Scribal competence included copying, calculation, lexical knowledge and genre conventions, not merely decoding signs.
claims.counterevidence: Curriculum differed by period, place and career path.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: Access was restricted and socially consequential, but no reliable percentage for literacy or a universal male-only rule can be derived.
claims.counterevidence: Named female scribes and elite women exist in some periods; corpus is not population-representative.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: House F at Old Babylonian Nippur provides an unusually contextualized household training sequence, not proof of a universal Mesopotamian school system.
claims.counterevidence: Its more than 1,400 tablets make the sequence unusually rich but also locally exceptional.
claims.narrative_implication: Use House F as an illustrative, high-resolution anchor explicitly labeled non-representative of all periods.

claims.statement: Professional title, functional competence and broad literacy must be mapped separately; some later archives show on-the-job or non-professional use outside a single formal school track.
claims.counterevidence: Survival still favors administrative settings and trained writers.
claims.narrative_implication: Describe capabilities and work roles instead of assigning a modern literate/illiterate binary.

claims.statement: Named women and female-authored or female-voiced texts demonstrate access in some settings but cannot establish population rates or unmediated authorship.
claims.counterevidence: Scribal mediation, elite selection and uneven survival complicate attribution.
claims.narrative_implication: Use specific women only with period, role, mediation and representativeness labels.

claims.statement: P228744 is a fragmented Old Babylonian lexical school tablet excavated at Nippur and a witness to the OB Nippur Ura 03 composite Q000001.
claims.counterevidence: The obverse is missing and the record does not preserve detailed stratigraphy; formal school material cannot establish population-wide literacy.
claims.narrative_implication: Use as a representative case of formal lexical classification and copying within the Nippur training tradition only.

claims.statement: Lexical lists and bilingual curricula were key transmission infrastructure across regions and centuries.
claims.counterevidence: Surviving lists privilege formal training contexts.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.
